query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys originally produced as single‐phase solid solutions, even trace levels of interstitial impurities (such as oxygen and nitrogen) can, under prolonged high‐temperature exposure, segregate at grain boundaries and trigger the nucleation of brittle secondary phases. These phases then reduce overall toughness and promote brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase solid solution high‐entropy alloy containing trace interstitial impurities uniformly dispersed within the matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled variations in the impurity (O, N) content and subject the alloy to thermal aging at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 700°C) to promote impurity segregation.
generation.conditions: Testing under both room temperature and high operational temperatures (near 700°C) that are representative of demanding engineering service conditions, combined with mechanical loading regimes (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness tests).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and precipitation of brittle, impurity-induced secondary phases (or intermetallic compounds) at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature conditions, trace interstitial impurities migrate and segregate to grain boundaries, where they catalyze the nucleation of brittle secondary phases. These phases disrupt the ductile matrix by acting as stress concentrators, compromising plastic deformation mechanisms and leading to a transition from ductile to brittle failure under load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with elevated impurity levels or after prolonged aging will exhibit reduced toughness and a granular, intergranular fracture morphology, in contrast to highly pure or unaged samples that maintain a more ductile fracture behavior.
generation.baseline: An ultra-high-purity high-entropy alloy (or alloy in its as-cast, unaged state) that maintains a single-phase solid solution with uniform properties and exhibits high toughness under similar mechanical loads.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of prolonged exposure to high temperatures (~700°C) and mechanical loading typical of extreme service environments; it may not be valid for low-temperature conditions or if impurity levels remain below a critical threshold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold impurity concentration and the kinetics of phase segregation are not quantitatively defined, thus making it uncertain as to the precise aging time and impurity level needed to trigger significant brittleness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with deliberately elevated oxygen and nitrogen content and a control set with ultra-high purity. Subject both sets to thermal aging at 700°C for a predetermined period, followed by mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness and tensile tests). Assess the microstructure using advanced microscopy techniques (e.g., SEM, TEM) to detect any formation of brittle phases.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (via SEM) to observe intergranular vs. ductile features
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to identify the presence of secondary phases at grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if there is no statistically significant difference in toughness reduction or fracture behavior between the high-impurity and purified samples after identical aging treatments, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of impurity-induced brittle phases in the aged high-impurity samples.

cited_evidence.text:
Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time.
